papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Connected Technologies in Chronic Pain Management: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic pain affects over 1.5 billion people worldwide, facing persistent challenges in assessment subjectivity, treatment variability, and scalability (i.e., the limited ability to deliver individualized care to large populations within current clinical systems). Artificial intelligence (AI) and connected health technologies have transitioned from experimental tools to clinical reality in pain management.
OBJECTIVE: This scoping review maps current AI applications, identifies implementation gaps, and demonstrates the need for systematic technology integration in pain medicine.
METHODS: We conducted a targeted literature search across PubMed, Scopus, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. From 487 identified articles, 23 met inclusion criteria for a detailed analysis. A scoping review approach, following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, provided an integrative perspective on these rapidly evolving applications.
RESULTS: AI implementations span four domains: (1) objective pain assessment via multimodal analysis (facial recognition, neurophysiology, and imaging); (2) personalized treatment strategies using machine learning to optimize therapeutic responses; (3) predictive analytics for risk stratification (postoperative pain and opioid misuse); and (4) real-time monitoring through connected devices and closed-loop neuromodulation. Notable applications include AI-guided spinal cord stimulation and wearable-integrated pain profiling. Despite demonstrable clinical benefits across these domains, integration remains fragmented due to data governance challenges and educational gaps among practitioners.
CONCLUSIONS: AI is demonstrably improving chronic pain outcomes, yet integration remains fragmented due to data governance issues and educational gaps. Professional societies must establish specialized AI committees, clinical guidelines, and structured training. As this transformation occurs, pain specialists must lead this evolution rather than adapt reactively to external changes.

papers.title: Interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention: EEG evidence for joint modulation of late perceptual processing.
papers.abstract: Voluntary action shapes our perception through sensory predictions of its consequences. These predictions are thought to inhibit perceptual processing of predicted outcomes, leading to sensory attenuation. However, some studies have reported findings that contrast with this effect, suggesting that the influence of predictions may reflect, or interact with, attentional processes. Here, we investigated the interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention on early and late perceptual processing, with prediction and attention referring to the likelihood of a sensory event and its behavioral relevance, respectively. Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded while participants viewed two sequential gratings. The orientation of the first was either predicted and self-generated or unpredicted and externally generated. Participants judged the tilt direction of the second grating relative to the first but responded only when the grating appeared in a task-relevant color. EEG analyses revealed no modulation of early visual potentials (N1a), but modulations at later processing stages. Specifically, the P3b exhibited reduced amplitude for predicted compared to unpredicted stimuli, but only when they were task-relevant, whereas task-relevance enhanced the P3b only for unpredicted stimuli. Interestingly, multivariate pattern analysis showed significant temporal clusters for decoding the grating's orientation exclusively for predicted and task-relevant stimuli, although decoding performance did not significantly differ between conditions. Furthermore, predicted and task-relevant stimuli elicited faster behavioral responses, with prediction-related P3b latency differences correlating with reaction-time differences. Overall, converging findings from the P3b, multivariate, time-frequency and behavioral analyses provide suggestive evidence that top-down attention and action-based prediction may jointly facilitate late perceptual and decision-related processing.

papers.title: Contralateral piriform cortex alterations after surgery for temporal lobe epilepsy: A pilot MRI volumetry study.
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is increasingly conceptualized as a network disorder, with the piriform cortex as an implicated region. We characterized postoperative contralateral piriform cortex-cortical amygdala (PCA) structural and perfusion-related changes in a small seizure-free TLE cohort.
METHODS: Nine patients with drug-resistant TLE who underwent epilepsy surgery and achieved postoperative seizure freedom were included in this single-center pre-post pilot study. Bilateral PCA was manually delineated on 3D T1-weighted MRI using ITK-SNAP, and volumes were normalized to total intracranial volume derived from CAT12 segmentation. Eight atlas-derived contralateral temporal lobe regions were examined as exploratory regional-specificity comparisons. In patients with available pulsed arterial spin labeling (PASL), piriform and putaminal signal intensities were measured by region-of-interest analysis. Non-parametric paired tests were used; secondary and exploratory analyses were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure.
RESULTS: Normalized to total intracranial volume (TIV) contralateral PCA volume decreased postoperatively (Wilcoxon Z = -2.073, exact two-tailed p = 0.039; r = 0.69). None of the eight atlas-derived contralateral temporal regions showed a significant pre-post volume change. Contralateral putamen-normalized piriform signal intensity did not change significantly (Z = -0.105, p = 0.917), and no secondary or exploratory analysis remained significant after FDR correction.
CONCLUSIONS: In this hypothesis-generating pilot cohort, contralateral PCA volume decreased after epilepsy surgery, whereas the PASL-derived signal-intensity measure did not show a corresponding group-level change. These observations do not establish a surgery-induced network mechanism and require confirmation in larger controlled longitudinal cohorts.

papers.title: Acetazolamide in drug-resistant epilepsy: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) remains a high-morbidity condition despite expanding antiseizure medications. Acetazolamide (ACZ), a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor introduced for epilepsy in the 1950s, has been largely displaced by newer agents and concerns about tolerance, but its low cost and pH-mediated mechanism support reassessment in select DRE contexts.
METHODS: We conducted a PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA-S-informed systematic review of clinical studies evaluating ACZ as mono- or adjunctive therapy for drug-resistant or refractory epilepsy through May 11, 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using Newcastle-Ottawa and ROBINS-I frameworks. To quantify treatment efficacy random-effects generalized linear mixed-model meta-analyses estimated seizure freedom and ≥50% responder rate.
RESULTS: Twenty-six studies were included. The pooled seizure-freedom proportion was 25.7% (95% CI, 15.8%-38.9%; k = 20; I² = 89.5%) and ≥50% responder proportion 67.5% (95% CI, 48.2%-82.2%; k = 26; I² = 96.7%). Leave-one-out analysis did not identify a single influential study nor did exploratory meta-regression show a significant age-response correlation. Phenotype-specific and narrative findings demonstrated more consistent response in certain catamenial, spike-wave, photosensitive, genetic, and metabolic epilepsy contexts. Metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis, and treatment discontinuation were comparatively uncommon, whereas adverse effects were predominantly tolerability-related.
CONCLUSION: ACZ retains a measurable but selective antiseizure signal in DRE. However, limitations in decades-old reporting, considerable between-study heterogeneity, limited controlled clinical evidence, and modest sample sizes in phenotype-specific cohorts require researchers to interpret the evidence with caution. Nevertheless, ACZ's observed clinical activity, low cost, and distinct mechanism of action make it a promising candidate for prospective studies to identify responsive epilepsy types, assess the durability of benefit, and redefine its place in modern epilepsy care.

papers.title: Network-guided Thalamic Neuromodulation for Epilepsy.
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review takes a network-based perspective on thalamic neuromodulation for epilepsy, examining how each target (e.g., anterior (ANT), centromedian (CM), and pulvinar (PUL) thalamic nuclei) engage distinct seizure networks, what evidence supports each, and how stimulation/electrophysiologic mapping can guide individualized targeting rather than a fixed, syndrome-based approach.
RECENT FINDINGS: Randomized and prospective trials have expanded the evidence for ANT and CM stimulation, while emerging data support the pulvinar as a target for posterior quadrant and temporal lobe epilepsies. Syndrome-specific sweet-spot analyses reveal distinct optimal sites within the CM for LGS and IGE. Thalamic sEEG with single-pulse stimulation and trials of DBS-style stimulation now enables characterization of seizure network engagement and identification of acute biomarkers that may inform target and parameter selection. Multi-target strategies combining thalamic nuclei, or thalamic and cortical leads, show preliminary promise for broadly distributed seizure networks. No single thalamic target is uniformly effective across epilepsy types; optimal targeting requires individualized, network-informed characterization. This supports a shift toward connectomic and individualized approaches, with future work needed to refine target selection, stimulation paradigms, and individualized optimization using clinical outcomes and electrophysiological biomarkers.

papers.title: What happens in vagus.
papers.abstract: The parasympathetic nervous system is phylogenetically ancient. In humans, the vagus nerve is the brain's only pathway for bidirectional parasympathetic signaling with the thorax, abdomen, and upper pelvis. Unsurprisingly, the vagus nerve has played a significant role in scientific discovery and therapeutic applications, attracting the attention of Galen, Darwin, and Pavlov, among others. For example, Otto Loewi used the vagus nerve to gather data that confirmed Santiago Ramón y Cajal's Neuron Doctrine. This intensive focus has led to a number of clinical advances related to vagus nerve function, including theories about mind-body connections. Interestingly, reducing vagus nerve activity has been a successful strategy for some clinical conditions, such as peptic ulcer disease and obesity. In other conditions, increasing vagus nerve activity has been successful at improving patient outcomes, for example, in refractory seizures, drug-resistant depression, and stroke recovery; in each of these three conditions, the FDA has approved vagus nerve stimulation as a therapeutic intervention. Potential future developments in the therapeutic modulation of vagus nerve activity are discussed, including its role in perinatal brain development; manipulation of the vagus nerve as a portal for CNS access, as suggested in Parkinson's disease; and closed-loop systems that modulate vagus nerve activity in response to measurement of various forms of signaling, an approach that would be aided by the capacity to directly measure activity in individual vagus nerves.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted categorization of interictal abnormalities in adult long-term electroencephalographic monitoring: Comparable diagnostic accuracy with marked efficiency gain.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Artificial intelligence (AI) classifies routine electroencephalograms (EEGs) with expert-level accuracy, but interpretation of long-term EEG monitoring (LTM) remains reliant on time-intensive visual review. We evaluated whether autoSCORE, a clinically approved implementation of SCORE-AI integrated into an EEG reader, achieves expert-level diagnostic accuracy for LTM interpretation and whether expert-supervised use reduces review time versus conventional analysis.
METHODS: A fixed-and-frozen AI model was tested on an independent single-center dataset of 78 adult patient LTM recordings (52 normal, 26 abnormal), with epilepsy monitoring unit discharge diagnosis as the external reference standard. The AI model was benchmarked against two expert panels (three readers each); Panel 1 reviewed autoSCORE EEG detections (hybrid approach), and Panel 2 interpreted full recordings (conventional approach). Diagnostic accuracy and time to diagnostic decision were assessed for fully automated, hybrid, and conventional approaches. Interrater reliability (Gwet's AC1) was evaluated for hybrid and conventional interpretation.
RESULTS: Interrater reliability was significantly higher for hybrid than conventional approach (AC1 = .81, 95% confidence interval [CI] = .73-.89 vs. AC1 = .43, 95% CI = .32-.53; p < .001). Review time was markedly reduced (median [interquartile range (IQR)] = 2.2 [.5-4.3] vs. 52.4 [33.2-62.9] min, mean [95% CI] = 2.9 [2.5-3.2] vs. 50.8 [46.5-55.2] min, p < .001), a 95.8% median reduction (IQR = 95.6-96.3). Diagnostic performance comparisons were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni procedure across all 63 tests. The hybrid approach showed significantly higher sensitivity than conventional interpretation (.88, 95% CI = .77-.97 vs. .69, 95% CI = .57-.81; adjusted p = .006). Its numerically higher diagnostic accuracy versus conventional interpretation (.75, 95% CI = .66-.83 vs. .68, 95% CI = .61-.74) was nonsignificant after correction (adjusted p > .99). Hybrid approach diagnostic accuracy was significantly greater than fully automated analysis (.75, 95% CI = .66-.83 vs. .55, 95% CI = .44-.65; adjusted p < .001).
SIGNIFICANCE: Expert oversight of AI-assisted categorization of interictal epileptiform and nonepileptiform EEG abnormalities improves interrater reliability and efficiency, increases diagnostic sensitivity versus conventional interpretation, and increases diagnostic accuracy versus fully automated analysis in adult LTM.

papers.title: Multimodal modeling of the ictal onset zone in refractory insular epilepsy and seizure outcome of magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial therapy: A pediatric single-center retrospective study.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study was undertaken to evaluate seizure outcomes after magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (MRgLITT) in children with insular epilepsy and to assess how the extent of ablation overlaps with multimodal definitions of the ictal onset zone (IOZ).
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, single-center study including consecutive pediatric patients treated with MRgLITT for insular epilepsy. All patients underwent presurgical evaluation including electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) and stereo-EEG (SEEG) were performed in negative-MRI cases. Epileptic zone was identified by visual analysis of SEEG recording. Postablation contrast-enhancing volumes were manually segmented and coregistered with IOZ estimates derived from Multi-centre Epilepsy Lesion Detection (MELD) MRI analysis, FDG-PET voxel-based analysis, and the Epileptogenicity Index, when available. Spatial concordance between modalities was assessed using Dice similarity coefficients, and the proportion of each IOZ modality encompassed within the ablation volume was correlated with postoperative seizure outcomes (International League Against Epilepsy classification).
RESULTS: Eight children (median age = 10.4 years, range = 2.3-17) were included, with a median postoperative follow-up of 38 months. Two patients had insular tumors, and both achieved seizure freedom after complete ablation. Among the six MRI-negative patients, FDG-PET revealed insular hypometabolism in four, MELD detected a median of one insular cluster (range 1-3), and SEEG identified focal insular ictal activity in three cases. Overall, four negative-MRI patients achieved seizure freedom: three after MRgLITT alone and one after MRgLITT combined with frontal opercular resection. One transient postoperative aphasia was observed. Intermodality spatial concordance was low across all comparisons. A greater proportion of FDG-PET hypometabolism included in the ablation volume was associated with better seizure outcomes (p = .012).
SIGNIFICANCE: MRgLITT is an effective and safe treatment option for focal insular epilepsy in children, either as standalone therapy or in a combined approach. Optimal outcome depends on accurate preoperative delineation of the IOZ and its complete ablation.

papers.title: Circuit-constrained molecular neuroethology in the medicinal leech Hirudo verbana.
papers.journal: Journal of comparative physiology. A, Neuroethology, sensory, neural, and behavioral physiology
papers.abstract: Medicinal leeches have long served as classic systems in comparative neuroethology because individual neurons can be identified across animals and linked to well-defined behaviors. This review argues that Hirudo verbana is now positioned for a new phase in which this identified-cell framework can be connected directly to molecular mechanisms. We first outline the organization and experimental accessibility of the leech nervous system, then evaluate genomic and transcriptomic resources as tools for testing physiologically constrained hypotheses rather than as endpoints in themselves. We focus on selected problems in which behavior, identified neurons, and molecular candidates can be brought into close alignment: sensory encoding, serotonergic state-dependent gating, multifunctional behavioral circuits, heartbeat rhythm generation, and endocannabinoid-dependent plasticity. Across these examples, the comparative value of Hirudo verbana lies not in nervous-system simplicity alone, but in interpretability: receptors, ion channels, pumps, peptides, gap-junction proteins, and metabolic enzymes can be examined in relation to cellular and circuit operations already defined by physiology. Future progress will require tighter integration of circuit-defined phenotypes with cell-resolved transcriptomics, spatial localization, targeted perturbation, and quantitative modeling. This circuit-constrained strategy positions Hirudo verbana as a valuable bridge between classical identified-cell neuroethology and molecular tests of circuit physiology.

papers.title: Neurovascular coupling in simultaneous EEG-fNIRS studies: A scoping review of analytical frameworks and clinical applications.
papers.abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) have been used across cognitive and physiological states and in diverse clinical populations. However, the interpretation of cross-modal coupling remains difficult because findings from different analytical frameworks, populations, and experimental conditions have not been systematically mapped. This scoping review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO, and IEEE Xplore were searched through February 10, 2026, for studies that quantitatively related simultaneously recorded EEG and fNIRS signals. Two reviewers independently screened the records. Findings were synthesized narratively, and analytical pipelines were mapped across the signal domain, feature extraction, coupling metric, and temporal lag handling. Fifty-seven studies were included. Amplitude-based studies related event-related potentials and oscillatory EEG features to focal hemodynamic responses, with associations varying across electrophysiological features, cortical regions, and task conditions. Frequency- and scale-specific analyses identified band-dependent relationships, while coupling at ultra-slow scales showed sensitivity to vascular and systemic physiological influences. Studies that explicitly modeled timing identified several-second offsets in some paradigms, while directional estimates varied across tasks and recording states. Network analyses showed partial and context-dependent correspondence between EEG- and fNIRS-derived measures, while model-based approaches characterized multivariate and predictive cross-modal relationships. Across frameworks, observed coupling differed with recording state, frequency band, cortical region, and temporal lag handling rather than representing a single quantity. Clinical findings were heterogeneous, and most condition-specific patterns were supported by small and methodologically diverse evidence bases. These findings support framework-matched analysis and pipeline-explicit reporting when interpreting EEG-fNIRS coupling.

papers.title: An efficient convolutional neural network model for classifying positive affective states from EEG data considering sleep condition.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The recognition of affective states from EEG recordings considering the sleep condition can be an important supporting tool in therapy and in the treatment of psychological or psychiatric disorders.
NEW METHOD: Since sleep deprivation changes EEG characteristics, a two-stage framework is developed for affective state classification. First, a classification between "Normal Sleep" (NS) and "Sleep-Deprived" (SD) is conducted using resting-state EEG data. The data are then fed into one of two newly proposed, lightweight Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to recognize four affective states.
RESULTS: In the first stage, CNN-BiLSTM achieves 95.96% accuracy under window-level splitting and 70.46% under subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation, while in the second stage the proposed models achieve 93.40% (NS) and 90.95% (SD) under window-level splitting, and 38.98% (NS) and 38.97% (SD) under cross-validation. The lower subject-independent accuracies reflect the class imbalance and the clustering of scores near the class boundaries, which make cross-subject four-class generalization challenging.
COMPARISON WITH EXISTING METHODS: As existing studies mostly classify momentary emotions without addressing sleep conditions, direct comparison with prior work is difficult; we therefore benchmarked our framework against several established baseline models, including SqueezeNet, EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest.
CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that considering physiological states can improve multi-class classification of affective states from time-varying neurophysiological signals such as EEG. The framework performs strongly under window-level evaluation, whereas its performance under the stricter subject-independent setting is more limited and should be interpreted accordingly. It can nonetheless contribute to more comprehensive research in affective neuroscience.

papers.title: Efficacy of Lactobacillus reuteri as an adjunctive therapy for seizure control and quality of life in pediatric drug-resistant epilepsy: A prospective interventional study.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) remains a critical challenge in pediatric neurology, profoundly impacting cognitive development and health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Given the role of the gut-microbiota-brain axis in neuromodulation, probiotics have emerged as a potential adjunctive therapy. This study assessed changes in seizure frequency and HRQOL and evaluated the safety of Lactobacillus reuteri supplementation on seizure frequency and HRQOL in children with DRE.
METHODS: In this prospective, single-arm, before-after interventional trial, 75 children (aged 3-18 years) with confirmed DRE were enrolled. Participants received daily oral L. reuteri (1 ×10 9  CFU) for 12 weeks alongside their stable anti-seizure medication (ASM) regimens. The primary outcome was HRQOL measured by the Persian-validated QOLCE-55 questionnaire. Secondary outcomes included seizure frequency, recorded prospectively using standardized caregiver seizure diaries. Statistical analyses utilized paired-sample t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with effect sizes calculated to quantify the magnitude of within-participant changes.
RESULTS: Seventy-one patients completed the study (mean age 7.26 ± 3.33 years; 53.5% male). The cohort showed heterogeneous seizure phenotypes and underlying etiologies. Total HRQOL scores increased from 33.75 ± 4.92 at baseline to 34.23 ± 4.97 after the intervention (absolute change, 0.48 points; p < 0.001), with a small-to-moderate standardized effect size (d = 0.40). However, this change was substantially below the 10-13-point MCID range used in the sample-size rationale. Median seizure frequency changed from 32 (IQR: 15-84) to 30 (IQR: 14-80) episodes per 3 months (p = 0.001; r = 0.39). Four patients (5.6%; 95% CI, 1.6-13.8%) experienced a reduction of more than 50% in seizure frequency. Adverse events were reported in 11.3% of participants and were mild and transient, with no treatment discontinuations.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm before-after study, statistically significant within-participant changes in HRQOL and seizure frequency were observed during the 12-week period following adjunctive L. reuteri supplementation. However, the absolute magnitude of these changes was modest and their clinical significance remains uncertain. Because there was no concurrent placebo control group, the observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to L. reuteri supplementation. Larger, adequately powered placebo-controlled randomized trials are needed to determine whether L. reuteri provides a clinically meaningful benefit in pediatric drug-resistant epilepsy.

papers.title: Combining responsive neurostimulation with resection or ablation for treatment of epilepsy: a multicenter experience.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Despite advances in surgical and neuromodulatory treatments, a substantial proportion of patients with drug-resistant epilepsy remain ineligible for standalone resection or ablation. Combining resection or laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) with responsive neurostimulation (RNS) has emerged as a promising approach for patients with multifocal seizure onset or eloquent cortex involvement. However, the clinical impact of combination surgery remains poorly characterized. The aim of this study was to characterize the clinical rationale and surgical decision-making used across multiple high-volume epilepsy centers performing combination surgeries, and to evaluate the seizure outcomes and safety profile associated with this approach.
METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with drug-resistant epilepsy who underwent RNS implantation in combination with resection or LITT at 9 epilepsy centers and had ≥ 1 year of follow-up. Demographic, clinical, surgical, and seizure outcome data were collected. The primary outcome was seizure reduction at 1 year. Secondary outcomes included the Clinical Global Impression and adverse events.
RESULTS: Overall, 73 patients (40 male, mean age 34 years) with a mean epilepsy duration of 21 years were included in this analysis. The most common etiology was unknown (37%), followed by cortical malformation (16%). Most patients experienced focal impaired consciousness (FIC, 78%) and focal to bilateral tonic-clonic (FBTC, 70%) seizures. Prior resection was performed in 23%. Combination procedures were performed on the same day in 89% of patients. RNS implantation was concurrent with resection in 92% and with LITT in 8.2% of patients. Neocortical and mesial temporal regions accounted for 61% of resection/ablation targets. More than two-thirds of RNS leads were subdural strips, most commonly in the left hemisphere (73%). Indications for the combined approach included eloquent cortex involvement (67%) and multifocal seizure onset (33%) or both (9.6%). At 1 year, mean seizure reductions were 53% for focal impaired, 69% for FIC, and 67% for FBTC seizures. Overall, 48% of patients had at least a 6-month period of seizure freedom, and 4 patients had no seizures after surgery. Significant global clinical improvement (much or very much improved) was observed in 79% of patients. Three patients experienced infection, and 1 patient died due to causes unrelated to surgical treatment (sudden unexpected death in epilepsy).
CONCLUSIONS: Combined RNS with resection or ablation might provide meaningful seizure control in complex drug-resistant epilepsy with acceptable safety profiles. These findings describe current practice and support further investigation of hybrid surgical strategies in patients with challenging seizure networks as a potential treatment strategy.

papers.title: More Than a Daughter: Margaret A. Lennox-Buchthal (1913-2001), Epileptologist.
papers.abstract: In a 2010 book chapter on the pioneering encephalographer Mary A.B. Brazier, PhD (1904-1995), a photo of a smiling woman is labeled "Margaret Lennox-Buchthal, wife of Fritz, daughter of William Lennox." Yet, like most women, Margaret Lennox-Buchthal, MD (1913-2001), was more than a wife and a daughter. She was an assistant professor at the Yale School of Medicine and associate professor at the University of Copenhagen Institute of Neurophysiology, and she was editor-in-chief of the journal  Epilepsia  (1969-1975). Her work had a lasting impact on our current concept of and approach to febrile seizures. She advocated for people with epilepsy and challenged stigmas as an educated divorced woman with a diagnosis of epilepsy. The story of Lennox-Buchthal's life illustrates the unsung roles women played in medicine and research in the mid-1900s, and how their achievements continue to be eclipsed by the men in their lives.

papers.title: Reversal of refractory epilepsy in an adult with GAMT deficiency: A case report and comparative literature review.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive creatine biosynthesis disorder. Reports specifically focusing on adult patients remain scarce.
METHODS: We report a 52-year-old female (the oldest documented case of GAMT deficiency to date) presenting with severe intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and adult-onset disease progression. Whole-exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous GAMT variants (c.265_267del and c.253G>T), and magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed cerebral creatine depletion. Remarkably, initiating oral creatine supplementation at age 52 achieved complete seizure freedom, normalization of the electroencephalogram (EEG), and significant motor function recovery.
RESULTS: A comprehensive review revealed that untreated adult patients face a high risk of progressive neurological deterioration. Compared to the pediatric cohort, adults exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of movement disorders (69.2% vs. 33.1%, p < 0.001) and a trend toward a higher prevalence of epilepsy (92.3% vs. 74.2%). Especially, atonic seizures (drop attacks) are particularly characteristic of adult GAMT deficiency, with EEGs frequently demonstrating background slowing, multifocal epileptiform discharges, and electrodecremental patterns.
SIGNIFICANCE: This study underscores that continuous disease progression and prolonged neurotoxicity still could compromise the well-being of adult GAMT deficiency patients. Accurate diagnosis is essential for adults presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) phenotype, as even late treatment for GAMT deficiency can still dramatically alleviate the epileptic burden and reverse motor decline.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: We report the oldest known adult diagnosed with GAMT deficiency. Our case demonstrates that starting creatine treatment even at age 52 can dramatically reduce seizures and restore motor function. Literature shows that untreated adults suffer from more severe epilepsy and movement disorders than children, with symptoms worsening over time. These findings highlight the critical need for genetic testing in adults with unexplained severe epilepsy; timely creatine supplementation can halt cognitive decline and significantly restore quality of life.

papers.title: Frequent involvement of cingulate and insulo-opercular regions in sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy: A multimodal presurgical study.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) is classically considered a frontal lobe epilepsy; however, accumulating evidence suggests that hypermotor seizures may arise from multiple frontal and extrafrontal regions. We characterized the anatomical distribution of best available localizations in patients with SHE using multimodal presurgical data.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 17 patients with clinically diagnosed SHE who underwent comprehensive evaluation, including long-term video-electroencephalographic (EEG) monitoring, 3-T high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, and, where indicated, magnetoencephalography, stereo-EEG (SEEG), and surgical assessment. Best available anatomical localizations were assigned using a hierarchical multimodal framework incorporating surgical, SEEG, and concordant noninvasive findings. Their anatomical distribution was subsequently assessed at the cohort level.
RESULTS: Sixteen patients (94.1%) had an assigned best available localization. Cingulate or insulo-opercular regions were involved in 11 of 16 patients (68.8%), whereas the remaining cases were localized to other frontal regions. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to 10 patients with SEEG-defined and/or surgically supported localizations, six involved cingulate or insulo-opercular regions. All patients were MRI-negative. In contrast, MRI-positron emission tomography fusion provided regionally informative anatomical findings in 16 of 17 cases and contributed to multimodal localization. Interictal epileptiform discharges were identified in 15 patients, whereas regionally informative ictal scalp EEG patterns were observed in eight; ictal interpretation was frequently limited by rapid propagation, movement-related artifacts, and delayed EEG onset. Focal cortical dysplasia-related histopathological findings were identified in five of seven resected specimens, whereas interpretation in two was limited by prior thermocoagulation.
SIGNIFICANCE: These descriptive findings indicate that cingulate and insulo-opercular regions were frequently represented among the identified localizations in this presurgical cohort. Multimodal evaluation integrating electroclinical, imaging, and invasive findings may support presurgical localization in MRI-negative SHE.

papers.title: Empagliflozin in Lafora disease: A first-in-human 6-month pilot study with electroclinical and FDG-PET findings.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Lafora disease (LD) is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative epilepsy with no approved treatments. Empagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, has shown neuroprotective actions in preclinical models through modulation of glycogen metabolism, induction of a pseudo-ketogenic state, improved mitochondrial efficiency, and reduction of excitatory neurotransmission. Based on this rationale, we conducted a first-in-human pilot study of empagliflozin in two genetically confirmed LD patients.
METHODS: Two patients with genetically confirmed LD received empagliflozin 10 mg/day for 6 months. Serial assessments included safety and tolerability, seizure frequency, myoclonus severity, electroencephalographic findings, neuropsychological and motor evaluations, brain MRI, and quantitative FDG-PET with regional Z-score analysis.
RESULTS: Empagliflozin was safe and well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Seizure frequency, myoclonus, and overall clinical status remained largely stable over 6 months, although some neuropsychological and motor measures showed variable changes between patients. EEG background activity and spike index were largely unchanged. Brain MRI showed stable mild cortical atrophy in both patients. In contrast, FDG-PET revealed progressive and spatially expanding cerebral hypometabolism in both patients, with worsening regional Z-scores, particularly in the parietal and precuneus regions.
SIGNIFICANCE: In this first-in-human, 6-month pilot study, empagliflozin showed acceptable short-term safety and feasibility in LD, but no definitive conclusions on efficacy can be drawn. The dissociation between relative electroclinical stability and progressive metabolic impairment suggests that quantitative FDG-PET may represent a sensitive biomarker for monitoring disease trajectory in this ultra-rare epilepsy.

papers.title: A GRAPH CONVOLUTION BASED DUAL-BRANCH NETWORK FOR DECODING OF UPPER-LIMB MOTOR IMAGERY EEG SIGNALS.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Analysing motor imagery EEG signals using conventional Euclidean feature computation is challenging due to low spatial resolution, non-stationarity, and complex inter-channel dependencies, which limit robust subject-independent generalization in brain-computer interface systems.
NEW METHOD: This study proposes a graph-based convolutional framework for subject-independent decoding of upper-limb motor imagery. The model integrates graph convolution with skip connections and handcrafted time-frequency features, together with parallel spatial and temporal convolutional pathways. Graph convolution captures functional connectivity between electrodes, while convolutional modules enhance spatial-temporal representation learning. Subject-independent evaluation is ensured using Stratified Group K-Fold (SGKF) and Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) validation protocols.
RESULTS: The framework was evaluated on the PhysioNet, BCI IV-2a, and BCI IV-2b datasets using multiple electrode configurations. For the PhysioNet dataset, three upper-limb classes were considered, achieving SGKF accuracies of 86.42%, 91.01%, and 93.91% using 64, 21, and 5 electrodes, respectively, and LOSO accuracies of 92.25%, 95.72%, and 96.01%. On the BCI IV-2a dataset, SGKF accuracies of 86.13%, 89.01%, and 92.33% were obtained, with LOSO accuracies reaching 97.12% using five electrodes. For the BCI IV-2b dataset, accuracies of 88.60% (SGKF) and 93.35% (LOSO) were achieved using only three electrodes.
COMPARISON WITH EXISTING METHODS: The proposed graph-based framework demonstrates competitive performance to representative graph-based methods while requiring fewer trainable parameters and EEG electrodes.
CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate that graph-based deep learning enables accurate, subject-independent motor imagery decoding with reduced model complexity and minimal electrode usage, supporting practical and resource-efficient brain-computer interface systems.

papers.title: Does delayed removal of stereo-EEG electrodes following radiofrequency thermocoagulation increase haemorrhage?
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RF-TC) is used in the assessment and treatment of medically refractory epilepsy, typically with electrode removal immediately following ablation. Our SEEG-guided RF-TC protocol includes the option of three further days of recording following thermocoagulation, prior to electrode removal. It is not known whether delayed removal of electrodes following RF-TC may increase the risk of haemorrhage.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the rate and volume of intracranial haemorrhage with immediate versus delayed electrode removal following RF-TC.
METHODS: 217 SEEG electrodes from 16 consecutive patients were retrospectively reviewed for haemorrhage. 3D T1-weighted (T1w) and Susceptibility Weighted (SWI) imaging were reviewed for haemorrhage along the electrode tract and at the site of RF-TC. The primary outcome measure was the per-electrode volume of T1w detectable haemorrhage at the site of RF-TC in electrodes removed immediately after RF-TC, compared to electrodes removed 3-days after RF-TC. Secondary outcomes compared the incidence and volume of T1w haemorrhage along the electrode tract in thermocoagulated versus non-thermocoagulated electrodes, presumed due to reflect haemorrhage from electrode insertion/removal. We also describe the temporal evolution of the MRI appearance of haemorrhage following SEEG-guided RF-TC.
RESULTS: No clinically significant haemorrhages occurred. At the site of RF-TC a small amount of blood product is universally present but there was no significant difference in per-electrode haemorrhage volume following delayed (93.8 ± 39.8 mm 3 ; ~diameter 5.6 mm) and immediate (80.0 ± 37.5 mm 3 ; ~ diameter 5.3 mm) removal of electrodes (Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.10). At the cortical surface there was no significant difference in the rate of T1w haemorrhage between thermocoagulated and non-thermocoagulated electrodes (63.1% vs 52.5%, p = 0.12, chi-squared).
CONCLUSION: Delayed removal of electrodes post-RF-TC allows assessment of response to RFA and the opportunity for further thermocoagulation if necessary. This exploratory study found no significant increase in haemorrhage volume with delayed electrode removal following RF-TC but a larger study would be required to definitively estimate haemorrhage risk.

papers.title: Beyond seizure control: Non-seizure-related outcomes in focal-onset epilepsy treated with adjunctive cenobamate. Third interim results from the BLESS study.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Cenobamate is approved for treatment of focal seizures in adults, but evidence on non-seizure outcomes remains limited. This interim statistical analysis of the cenoBamate in aduLts with focal-onsEt SeizureS (BLESS) study evaluated patient- and clinician-reported outcomes for up to 52 weeks of cenobamate treatment.
METHODS: BLESS is an observational, retrospective and prospective cohort study designed to assess the real-world effectiveness and safety of adjunctive cenobamate in adults with uncontrolled focal epilepsy. Outcomes included patient-reported health-related quality of life, sleepiness, anxiety, mood, and global functioning assessed by the 31-item Quality of Life in Epilepsy Inventory (QOLIE-31), the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and the Clinical Global Impression (CGI) scales.
RESULTS: A total of 377 participants were included. Among subjects with an available score at 12 (n = 197), 24 (n = 363), and 52 (n = 197) weeks, the QOLIE-31 overall score remained stable. Subjects with sustained seizure freedom at 24 weeks showed a significantly higher QOLIE-31 overall score (p = 0.041) and cognitive functioning scores (p = 0.019) compared with those who did not reach sustained seizure freedom. More than 68% of participants had normal daytime sleepiness (total ESS score 0-10) and did not report anxiety or depression according to the HADS-A and HADS-D subscales at each assessment up to 52 weeks. Clinicians rated 91.3% (n/N = 179/196), 85.7% (n/N = 300/350), and 87.4% (n/N = 167/191) of subjects as improved for their overall condition from the initiation of treatment according to the CGI-Improvement or change (CGI-I) scale, at 12, 24, and 52 weeks.
SIGNIFICANCE: This interim analysis provides preliminary descriptive evidence on non-seizure outcomes in subjects treated with adjunctive cenobamate. Patient-reported outcome scores remained stable from 12 weeks and up to 52 weeks, consistent with preserved overall well-being. Better quality of life and cognitive functioning emerged in sustained vs non-sustained seizure-free participants. Based on clinicians' judgment, there was signal of improvement in overall condition compared to baseline in most treated subjects throughout the observation period.

papers.title: Impact of sedation on the reliability of magnetoencephalographic language mapping in pediatric epilepsy.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) language mapping in pediatric epilepsy frequently requires sedation, which may alter cortical physiology and compromise the reliability of language lateralization. We hypothesized that sedation disrupts coupling between early auditory processing and higher order language networks, reducing the interpretability of laterality metrics.
METHODS: Sixty-nine pediatric patients undergoing presurgical MEG evaluation were analyzed, including 32 nonsedated and 37 sedated participants. Auditory evoked field responses were quantified using the M200/M100 amplitude ratio and interhemispheric asymmetry. Language laterality indices (LIs) were derived from a continuous recognition memory paradigm, and source localization was performed using Fast-VESTAL.
RESULTS: Sedation preferentially suppressed late auditory responses, reflected by a significant reduction in the M200/M100 ratio (p < .001) and increased interindividual variability. Despite preserved early sensory responses, auditory-language coupling was numerically attenuated under sedation. Notably, low M200/M100 ratios were frequently associated with highly lateralized LI values, suggesting reduced physiological reliability and the potential for "false certainty" in language lateralization. Source imaging demonstrated preserved primary auditory cortical activity with reduced recruitment of higher order association networks in sedated participants.
SIGNIFICANCE: Sedation compromises the physiological reliability of MEG language lateralization by disrupting late auditory and association-level processing. The M200/M100 ratio provides a practical physiological marker for identifying cases in which laterality results should be interpreted with caution. These findings support a physiology-informed framework for improving the clinical interpretation of MEG language mapping in sedated pediatric patients, with direct implications for presurgical planning in pediatric epilepsy.

papers.title: Change in clobazam pharmacokinetics after introduction of cenobamate.
papers.abstract: Cenobamate is a new antiseizure medication with an unusually high seizure-free rate, resulting in frequent use in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. Many of these patients are taking clobazam (CLB) at baseline. Cenobamate has important interactions with CLB, requiring CLB dose adjustment in conjunction with cenobamate titration. There is limited guidance on the optimal CLB dose adjustment after cenobamate introduction and titration. We measured levels of CLB and its active metabolite N-desmethylclobazam (N-CLB) before and after cenobamate titration in 10 subjects with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The mean CLB dose at baseline was 34.5 mg/day (range = 15-60 mg/day). We empirically started reducing the dose of CLB when starting 25 mg of cenobamate, then we cut the CLB dose down to 10 or 5 mg when reaching a cenobamate dose of 50 mg daily. The mean final dose of CLB was 9 mg (74% reduction). The average combined CLB + N-CLB level after cenobamate titration was 2191 μg/mL, not significantly different from baseline (2358 μg/mL). Although there may be individual variability, a 70%-74% CLB dose reduction may be appropriate to achieve an equivalent combined CLB + N-CLB level.

papers.title: CLSP-REQA: a real-time quality-aware closed-loop seizure prediction framework with Mamba-BiLSTM and confidence-gated intervention.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Reliable seizure prediction is a prerequisite for closed-loop neurostimulation therapy, yet existing methods rarely account for the variability in EEG signal quality encountered in real-world deployment, and the overwhelming majority adopt non-strict evaluation protocols that overestimate generalization performance.
METHODS: We propose CLSP-REQA (Closed-Loop Seizure Prediction with Real-time EEG Quality Assessment), a unified framework that embeds a lightweight signal quality estimator directly within the prediction pipeline. A Real-time EEG Quality Assessment (REQA) module runs in parallel with a Mamba-BiLSTM backbone, producing a scalar quality score  q  ∈ [0, 1] that modulates output confidence through a tiered non-linear fusion function (ECLO). We conducted dedicated experiments testing whether this learned score reflects genuine signal quality rather than a redundant proxy for the prediction task, and a sensitivity analysis of the fusion thresholds against standard calibration baselines. The framework was evaluated under strict cross-patient evaluation on the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG Database ( n  = 23 subjects, 198 seizures) and the SIENA Scalp EEG Database ( n  = 14 subjects, 47 seizures).
RESULTS: On CHB-MIT, CLSP-REQA achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.7426 ± 0.0199, exceeding the unadapted cross-patient baseline of 0.69 reported by Jemal et al., using only 16 EEG channels compared to 23 in prior work, and without requiring any target-patient data or domain adaptation. On SIENA, CLSP-REQA achieved an AUC of 0.7012 ± 0.0249, exceeding the best domain-adapted cross-patient result of 0.61 on the same dataset under a strictly harder information constraint, since domain adaptation methods are given access to unlabelled target-patient data that CLSP-REQA does not use.
DISCUSSION: The framework outputs a structured four-tuple 〈 p, q, c , Φ SHAP 〉 designed for compatibility with closed-loop neurostimulator interfaces. As both evaluation datasets are retrospective recordings from controlled hospital settings, we report this study as a feasibility demonstration rather than evidence of prospective, real-world clinical readiness, and the comparison with domain adaptation should not be read as unconditional superiority.

papers.title: Machine Learning Framework for Integration of Video and EEG Reveals Distinct Seizure Phenotypes in Mouse Models of Epilepsy.
papers.journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
papers.abstract: Video-electrocorticogram (VEEG) recordings are the gold-standard diagnostic tool for detecting and characterizing seizures in rodent models of seizure and epilepsy. Manual/visual scoring remains the prevailing strategy despite significant limitations. Alternatively, automated and semi-automated analyses have been applied to either EEG or video features alone but integrating these disparate data forms presents a challenge that has not been sufficiently addressed. Here, we introduce an integrated machine learning pipeline that jointly leverages EEG and behavioral video data to enable scalable and objective event classification. Integrated video-EEG analysis was initially validated using a well-established pharmacologically induced seizure paradigm in male mice, where overt generalized motor seizures provide a clear benchmark. We then tested the pipeline on a genetic mouse model of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) that displays a complex spike-wave discharge (SWD) seizure phenotype that poses significant challenges for traditional scoring methods. Machine learning-powered integrated analysis of video-EEG recordings outperformed unimodal EEG- or video-based approaches and performed favorably to experienced rodent EEG electrophysiologists while also uncovering distinct phenotypic relationships, including classes of atypical behavioral and typical non-behavioral SWD events. This framework provides a flexible tool for high-throughput, precise analysis of VEEG data, with potential to accelerate discovery in epilepsy and seizure research. Furthermore, this approach represents a generalizable strategy for the integration of diverse neurobehavioral time series data types. Significance Statement  Seizure detection in animal models of epilepsy has relied heavily on manual analysis of video-EEG recordings, a process that is slow and subjective. We present a machine learning pipeline that integrates EEG and video data from mice to classify seizures with high accuracy. This work was validated across two models, first a pharmacologically induced generalized seizure model, and second, a spontaneous spike-wave discharge (SWD) model in genetic epilepsy. Our approach detected events missed by human reviewers and revealed previously uncharacterized SWD subtypes distinguished by their behavior. By combining open-source tools in a flexible framework, this work lowers the barrier to high-throughput, unbiased seizure phenotyping, and also offers a broadly applicable strategy for linking neural activity to behavior in neuroscience research.

papers.title: Antibody-mediated encephalitides: distinct diseases with transdisciplinary implications.
papers.abstract: The discovery of antibody-mediated glial and neuronal disorders has transformed the diagnosis and treatment of neurological diseases previously considered idiopathic or not recognised as immune-mediated. Antibody-mediated disorders targeting glial aquaporin-4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein are distinct nosological entities, defined by specific targets, mechanisms, syndromes, and therapeutic implications. By contrast, antibody-mediated disorders targeting neuronal antigens (ie, autoimmune encephalitides) are still frequently analysed collectively, with data from different disorders pooled as if they represent a single disease rather than distinct entities. Evidence from anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, anti-LGI1 encephalitis, and anti-IgLON5 disease (used here as exemplars of autoimmune encephalitides) indicates that individual autoimmune encephalitides differ in demographics, triggers, mechanisms, clinical manifestations, post-acute trajectories, and treatment requirements. The broad, heterogeneous presentations of autoimmune encephalitides require coordinated multidisciplinary care within and beyond neurology, involving specialists in paediatrics, infectious diseases, epilepsy, movement disorders, sleep medicine, intensive care, cognitive rehabilitation, and other relevant disciplines. Such interdisciplinary collaboration facilitates the recognition of new diseases and elucidation of the causes of previously unclassified disorders. Improving patient care requires not only aetiological and mechanistic insight to enable development of targeted therapies but also strengthened cross-specialty expertise to optimise diagnosis and management.

papers.title: Reframing traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury as chronic multisystem disorders: toward integrated, long-term care.
authors: Global Coalition for TBI as a Notifiable and Chronic Condition
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) affect more than 220 million people worldwide and are associated with cardiometabolic, endocrine, neurological, and psychiatric sequelae for years to decades after an acute injury. However, most health systems still treat neurotrauma (TBI and SCI, collectively) as a time-limited event, leaving long-term surveillance of these patients fragmented or absent, which leads to preventable mortality and avoidable readmissions. TBI and SCI in adults should be reclassified as acute-onset multisystem chronic-risk conditions. Existing cardiovascular, endocrine, and psychiatric services do not capture neurotrauma-specific risks, including trauma-induced hypopituitarism, autonomic dysregulation, accelerated ageing, and cognitive-behavioural impairment, so neurotrauma care is best framed as a missing node in chronic neurological care. We propose a risk-stratified pathway of care navigation, multisystem screening, and telehealth; convergence with adjacent stroke, cardiometabolic, memory, psychiatric, pain, and epilepsy services; and the financing, workforce, and registry reforms needed to deliver measurable reductions in 5-year mortality, avoidable rehospitalisation, and long-term disability.

papers.title: Association Between Epilepsy and Young-Onset Dementia: Nationwide Data From France and Sweden.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Epilepsy is linked to late-onset dementia, but evidence for young-onset dementia (YOD; <65 years) is limited. We assessed the epilepsy-YOD association in France and Sweden and YOD risk after midlife epilepsy.
METHODS: We conducted 3 nationwide analyses. A French nested case-control analysis included patients with incident YOD aged 40-64 years, diagnosed between January 1, 2016, and December 31, 2018. Index date was the first YOD-related health care event; controls were risk-set matched on age, sex, and region. A Swedish nested case-control replication included patients with YOD diagnosed between January 1, 1987, and December 31, 2016, with matched controls. In both studies, epilepsy-related diagnoses and antiseizure medication (ASM) dispensations were assessed up to 10 years before index date. Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated with conditional logistic regression. A French retrospective cohort included adults aged 30-55 years with incident epilepsy in 2008, matched to individuals with prevalent epilepsy before 2008 or no epilepsy. The cohort index was the first ASM reimbursement in the incident epilepsy group or the matched date for comparators. Follow-up ended at YOD, death, or 10 years. We estimated 10-year cumulative incidence and adjusted (comorbidities, deprivation) hazard ratios (HRs), treating death as a competing event. Sensitivity analyses included lagged entry up to 5 years.
RESULTS: Case-control studies included 11,360 cases and 113,600 controls in France and 16,433 cases and 164,330 controls in Sweden. In France, 12.5% of YOD cases vs 1.2% of controls had previous epilepsy-related codes (adjusted OR 3.76, 95% CI 3.42-4.14), and 27.3% vs 10.3% had ASM dispensations (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.36-1.52). The French cohort included 12,901 individuals with incident epilepsy, 64,083 with prevalent epilepsy, and 129,010 without epilepsy (mean age 44.0 years; 55.5% female participants). Ten-year cumulative YOD incidence was 2.20% (95% CI 1.94-2.48) with incident epilepsy (adjusted HR compared with individuals without epilepsy 6.02, 95% CI 4.98-7.26), 1.74% (1.64-1.85) with prevalent epilepsy (adjusted HR 5.38, 95% CI 4.64-6.25), and 0.21% (0.19-0.24) without epilepsy. Associations attenuated with longer lags but persisted beyond 5 years.
DISCUSSION: Across 2 countries and complementary designs, epilepsy was strongly associated with YOD. Epilepsy conferred higher YOD risk in midlife, especially with multimorbidity, supporting epilepsy inclusion in YOD risk stratification and prevention.

papers.title: Passive Language Mapping With High-Gamma Modulations.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
papers.abstract: Passive language mapping using high-gamma modulation (HGM) has emerged as a valuable tool in both presurgical evaluation for epilepsy and neuroscientific discovery. HGM mapping leverages task-related synchronization in high-gamma frequencies to identify language areas without the risks associated with electrical stimulation mapping. This review outlines the principles and techniques used in the field of HGM-based mapping, including electrode types, referencing schemes, power analysis, and localization techniques. We survey a range of cognitive tasks-speech production, auditory processing, reading, and memory-that elicit language-related HGM responses and discuss their relevance to comprehensive language mapping. We examine perspectives on methodologic challenges, including artifact management, variability across patients, and spatial sampling. We assess validation studies comparing HGM with electrical stimulation mapping and neuropsychological outcomes, noting HGM's unique role in identifying language cortex in pediatric and cognitively impaired populations. Finally, we speculate on the future directions of the field, including integration with corticocortical evoked potentials and the potential for HGM-informed speech synthesis. As the field matures, HGM mapping is poised to contribute to improved clinical outcomes and enhance our understanding of the dynamics and development of the human language network.

papers.title: Open-Loop Deep Brain Stimulation Versus Closed-Loop Responsive Neurostimulation in Drug-Resistant Bitemporal Epilepsy: A Narrative Review.
papers.journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology
papers.abstract: Drug-resistant bitemporal epilepsy presents a therapeutic challenge when resective surgery is not feasible due to bilateral seizure onset or eloquent cortex involvement. Neuromodulation has emerged as an alternative, with open-loop deep brain stimulation (DBS) and closed-loop responsive neurostimulation (RNS) as implantable strategies. Comparative indications for modality selection remain unclear. A narrative review of articles published from January 2007 to January 2026 was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE. Approximately 120 articles were screened, and 39 studies were included. Due to heterogeneity in study design, findings were synthesized qualitatively. Both DBS and RNS significantly reduce seizure frequency in drug-resistant bitemporal epilepsy, with a median seizure reduction of approximately 60% to 75%. Seizure freedom, however, remained limited, reflecting the palliative nature of these treatments. Open-loop anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) DBS provides network-level modulation with low maintenance, while hippocampal DBS offers localized temporal inhibition. Conversely, closed-loop RNS delivers adaptive focal stimulation via real-time sensing and yields chronic intracranial electroencephalogram data. While both modalities show comparable efficacy, RNS may be advantageous in focal or asymmetric bitemporal epilepsy. Cognitive outcomes were favorable for both techniques, with RNS demonstrating the prevention of memory and language decline. Both DBS and RNS are palliative neuromodulatory options for patients in whom resective surgery is not feasible. Treatment selection should be individualized based on seizure network characteristics, laterality, monitoring needs, participation capacity, and cognitive considerations. The primary goal is to reduce seizure frequency and improve quality of life rather than to achieve seizure freedom. Future multicenter studies and biomarker-driven strategies are needed to refine selection and improve long-term outcomes.

papers.title: Limited sex-specific structural alterations across common epilepsies: A worldwide ENIGMA study.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Epilepsy is characterized by widespread cortical and subcortical structural alterations beyond the epileptic zone. Importantly, the clinical manifestation of epilepsy, including seizure types, psychiatric comorbidities, and treatment responses, has been shown to differ between sexes. However, sex differences in structural alterations in epilepsy are seldomly reported in neuroimaging studies, partly due to limited sample sizes and single-center designs. We therefore tested whether epilepsy-related structural alterations differ between males and females, and whether the associations between structural measures and clinical characteristics vary by sex.
METHODS: We analyzed clinician-assigned biological sex differences in common epilepsies and their related clinical variables using structural neuroimaging biomarkers in an international multicenter cohort of 1253 epilepsy patients and 1077 healthy controls. We studied cortical thickness and subcortical volume in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and genetic generalized epilepsy (GGE).
RESULTS: Both male and female patients with TLE showed widespread cortical and subcortical alterations in sex-stratified analyses, whereas GGE showed more extensive alterations in female patients and only subtle alterations in male patients. However, no significant sex-by-diagnosis interactions were identified in either the TLE (t = -2.153 to 1.705, all p FDR  >.05) or GGE (t = -1.797 to 2.774, all p FDR  >.05) cohort. Likewise, no significant interactions were found between sex and age at onset (t TLE  = -1.835 to 1.092, t GGE  = -2.394 to 1.392, all p FDR  >.05) or disease duration (t TLE  = -2.643 to 2.048, t GGE  = -1.234 to 2.017, all p FDR  >.05) in either patient group.
SIGNIFICANCE: Overall, although sex differences in behavioral and clinical outcomes of epilepsy have been consistently reported in previous studies, our results indicate that sex-related clinical differences in epilepsy are not strongly captured by macroscale structural magnetic resonance imaging measures, and may instead arise from hormonal, neurochemical, or functional-network mechanisms.

papers.title: Affective symptoms in focal epilepsy: A scoping review of localization and lateralizing findings.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract: Emotional experiences during focal seizures are often misinterpreted as psychiatric disorders. We aimed to evaluate symptoms involving affective symptoms at seizure onset. We aimed to identify the most prevalent affective symptoms at seizure onset and characterize their localizing and lateralizing value. We performed a scoping review based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses-extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. A systematic search identified records from 4 databases: PubMed, Embase, CINAHL (via EBSCOhost), and Web of Science. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts; discrepancies were resolved by consensus. This review focused on patients with focal seizures, as affective symptoms may occur in generalized epilepsies. The affective symptoms: fear, anxiety, panic, sadness, mystic, ecstatic, sexual, and mirth were identified, and semiology was evaluated in accordance with ILAE guidelines. Symptom onset, frequency, brain localization, and video-EEG monitoring technique were evaluated to assess localization and lateralization of regional networks. Scalp EEG, invasive EEG recordings, and electrical stimulation were analyzed. A total of 1276 documents were identified, with 98 studies included for review. Fear was the most frequently reported ictal emotion, identified in 274 patients (66%), predominantly in temporal lobe epilepsy. Sadness and sexual, ecstatic symptoms were also consistently associated with temporal networks. Mirth was more frequently reported with frontal onset seizures. Evidence, primarily from Class IV studies, reported right hemispheric predominance for ecstasy, mystic, and sexual symptoms at seizure onset. Ictal affective symptoms at seizure onset yield localizing information. The limbic system, especially the temporal lobe, followed by the frontal lobe, was the most common site of origin. Fear was the most common spontaneous and electrically elicited symptom, followed by anxiety. While bi-hemispheric lateralization occurred, right lateralization predominated. Recognizing paroxysmal affective symptoms as ictal phenomena may reduce misdiagnosis and aid presurgical evaluation in drug-resistant focal epilepsy.

papers.title: The basal ganglia and the epilepsies.
papers.abstract: The basal ganglia are an evolutionarily conserved neural circuit best known for the selection and sequencing of voluntary movement. Increasing evidence, however, indicates that these structures also play an important role in regulating pathological brain states, including seizures. Early pharmacological and lesion studies demonstrated that manipulation of basal ganglia output nuclei, particularly the substantia nigra pars reticulata, profoundly alters seizure susceptibility across multiple experimental models. Subsequent work expanded this view, revealing that several basal ganglia structures, including the striatum, subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, and superior colliculus, participate in a distributed network capable of modulating seizure initiation, propagation, and generalization. Modern systems neuroscience approaches have begun to define the specific cell types and projection-defined pathways through which these effects are mediated. Together, these findings support the concept that the basal ganglia function as a "seizure-gating" network that interacts with thalamocortical and brainstem arousal systems to regulate cortical synchronization. Understanding how these circuits influence seizure dynamics may enable new therapeutic strategies that strengthen endogenous seizure-suppressing networks rather than targeting the seizure focus alone. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: The basal ganglia are a group of deep brain structures best known for helping to start and stop movements. Over the past 40 years, research has shown that they also act as a brake on seizures. Studies across species demonstrate that "turning off" one of the main output structures of the basal ganglia, the substantia nigra pars reticulata, can stop many types of seizures. This review presents the "wiring diagram" of this brain circuit, including the effects of "turning on" and "turning off" individual brain regions and their connections on seizure initiation, propagation, and termination.

papers.title: Genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies in adulthood: Gaps in evidence and care.
papers.abstract: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a heterogeneous group of the most severe epilepsies, characterized by seizure onset and neurodevelopmental delay in infancy or childhood, often with additional neurological and systemic comorbidities. Up to 50% of cases have an identifiable genetic cause, with structural etiologies representing a small minority. Although associated with early mortality, many individuals now live into adulthood. Over the past 15 years, advances in genetic diagnosis and understanding of disease mechanisms have created realistic prospects of precision therapies, including gene and RNA therapies. The adult phase of DEEs remains poorly characterized, with limited observational evidence. Adults with DEEs are underrepresented in the literature and often excluded from clinical trials, despite ongoing drug-resistant epilepsy, evolving neurodevelopmental disability, and an increasing burden of comorbidities with age. In this narrative review, we discuss important aspects of care for adults with genetic DEEs, including genetic testing, comorbidities and treatment. We also review available natural history studies, recent clinical trials, and consider how emerging disease-modifying therapies may reshape adult phenotypes and redefine priorities for lifelong care. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a group of rare diseases that are often caused by genetic changes. They usually begin in childhood with severe epilepsy but can also affect learning, development, and overall health throughout life. This review examines the healthcare needs of adults with DEEs, highlights areas where more research is needed, and explores how new treatments may improve health and quality of life across the lifespan.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Microstate Dynamics and their Associations with Acclimatization Index and Serum Albumin in Healthy Adults with Chronic High-Altitude Exposure.
papers.abstract: High-altitude hypoxia has been examined with conventional electroencephalography (EEG), event-related potentials, and neuroimaging, but its association with millisecond-scale resting-state EEG microstate dynamics and peripheral physiology remains unclear. We studied healthy adults including 124 low-altitude (LA) participants (50 men, 74 women) and 174 high-altitude (HA) participants (42 men, 132 women; age 28.05 ± 8.59 years; age unavailable for LA). Coverage, duration, global explained variance (GEV), occurrence, and transition probabilities were extracted for four canonical microstates. LA-HA differences were tested using unadjusted linear models; within-HA associations among the high-altitude acclimatization index (AAI), serum albumin, and Microstate A-related indicators were examined using covariate-adjusted regressions and exploratory bootstrapped mediation analyses. Compared with LA participants, HA participants showed increased Microstate A duration and GEV, decreased occurrence, and unchanged coverage, together with reduced Microstate B-related indicators, enhanced Microstate C-related indicators, and increased A→B and A→C transitions. Within HA participants, AAI was negatively associated with serum albumin, and exploratory mediation analyses indicated indirect associations between AAI and Coverage A, Occurrence A, GEV A, and Microstate A-originating transitions through serum albumin. These findings suggest that chronic high-altitude exposure is associated with resting-state EEG microstate reorganization in healthy adults and that acclimatization-related individual differences may be linked to Microstate A dynamics through serum albumin-related peripheral status.

papers.title: Human-artificial intelligence collaboration for comanaging epilepsy in real time.
papers.abstract: One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures uncontrolled by medication, and implantable devices are a promising treatment. These devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but, like most medical devices, they cannot share this information with patients in real time. This is a missed opportunity for devices to learn from clinical events and teach patients how their behaviors affect their health. Here we present a device platform that converses with patients to help them manage their epilepsy. The inpatient prototype links scalp and intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) to a secure, large language model-based artificial intelligence (AI) that communicates bidirectionally through a smartphone app. The AI processes biomarkers of sleep, medication, cognition and seizure probability, notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector, reducing false alarms. We validated this platform in 13 patients who are undergoing video-EEG monitoring for epilepsy (scalp, n = 11; intracranial, n = 2). In a pseudoprospective simulation, seizure detectors improved precision from patient feedback alone, without expert intervention. We propose this system as a scalable, safeguarded platform for medical devices that can rapidly adapt to patient and provider needs across epilepsy and other medical conditions.

papers.title: Responsive Neurostimulation of the Centromedian Nucleus of the Thalamus for the Treatment of Drug-Resistant Idiopathic Generalized Epilepsy: A Retrospective Analysis of Efficacy and Exploratory Role of Different Stimulation Frequency Paradigms.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Closed-loop (responsive) neurostimulation (RNS) targeting the bilateral centromedian thalamic nucleus (CMN) is a safe and efficacious therapy for idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE). However, the optimal stimulation parameters have yet to be elucidated. The aims of this study were to review the efficacy of CMN-RNS in drug-resistant IGE and discuss the potential role of stimulation frequency in CMN-RNS programming.
METHODS: This study is a single-institution retrospective analysis of 10 patients with drug-resistant IGE who underwent CMN-RNS implantation. Initial therapy programming consisted of bipolar settings with opposite polarity between burst 1/2 and initial current 0.5 mA, charge density 0.5 μC/cm 2 , frequency 125 Hz, pulse width 160 μsec, and burst duration 500 msec. If patients experienced seizures or developed paresthesia with increasing charge density, they were transitioned to mid (10-100 Hz) or low frequency (<10 Hz) stimulation.
