papers.title: Default mode network mechanisms of trait rumination in treatment-resistant depression and rTMS: evidence from source-localized EEG.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Rumination is a transdiagnostic feature of multiple psychiatric disorders and is a critical risk factor for more severe episodes and poor treatment outcomes in treatment-resistant depression (TRD). Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) ameliorates both depressive and ruminative symptoms in TRD. While prior literature has linked rumination to abnormal default mode network (DMN) connectivity, the electrophysiological correlates of rumination in the DMN are not well understood.
METHODS: Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) data were examined in a cohort of 66 TRD subjects who underwent 30 sessions of rTMS treatment for TRD administered to left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). We employed source-localization and calculated four metrics of functional connectivity (Amplitude Envelope Correlation [AEC], weighted Phase Lag Index [wPLI], magnitude-squared coherence, and Spectral Correlation Coefficient [SCC]) across five frequency bands within the DMN to identify the neural correlates of rumination in TRD. Correction for multiple comparisons was performed using the Network Based Statistic (NBS).
RESULTS: Baseline severity of rumination and depression were positively correlated, but AEC alpha band connectivity was positively associated only with baseline rumination severity and not depression. Rumination severity prior to treatment was not associated with any other connectivity metric. Severity of rumination and depression decreased following rTMS treatment, but alpha AEC connectivity did not charge after 30 sessions of rTMS treatment.
CONCLUSION: Higher DMN connectivity, as measured by alpha-band AEC, is a stable trait-like neurophysiological marker of rumination that is not significantly affected by rTMS administered to left DLPFC.

papers.title: EMG-Driven Phase-Locked Spinal Cord Stimulation Physiologically Modulates Essential Tremor.
papers.journal: IEEE transactions on neural systems and rehabilitation engineering : a publication of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society
papers.abstract: Essential tremor (ET) is the most prevalent movement disorder, yet existing pharmacological and surgical treatments often lack efficacy or involve significant risks. Phase-locked neuromodulation offers a targeted approach to disrupt pathological oscillations, but its implementation through non-invasive spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) has remained largely unexplored. In this study, we present a novel closed-loop tSCS framework for ET based on real-time tremor phase estimation from surface electromyography (EMG). The system implements a Fourier Linear Combiner (FLC) algorithm to track the demodulated EMG signal sample-by-sample, enabling short-latency stimulation delivery while mitigating the phase lag inherent in traditional filtering or decomposition methods. The framework was validated in ET patients performing an isometric precision pinching task, with stimulation delivered across eight equidistant phases of the tremor cycle. The results demonstrate the technical feasibility of the system, which achieved a peak-to-trough tremor amplitude modulation of approximately 20% relative to the trial mean. Furthermore, the observation of phase-dependent frequency modulation in a small subset of participants suggested that tSCS may interact with tremorgenic timing mechanisms via spinal afferent pathways without compromising voluntary motor control. These findings provide an initial demonstration that closed-loop tSCS can produce phase-dependent modulation of tremor in individual patients, where physiological modulation is driven by the precise temporal synchronization of stimuli with the patient's underlying neurophysiology.

papers.title: Exploring medical food supplementation as an adjunct strategy for microbiota restoration and seizure reduction in CDKL5 deficiency disorder.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by early-onset, treatment-resistant seizures and severe neurodevelopmental impairment. Increasing evidence suggests that alterations in the gut-brain axis may contribute to disease pathophysiology, raising interest in microbiota-targeted interventions. In this study, we evaluated the effects of a prebiotic-based nutritional intervention on clinical outcomes, gut microbiota composition, and fatty acid profiles in individuals with CDD.
METHODS: Thirteen participants with drug-resistant epilepsy were enrolled (one male; median age, 12 years [IQR, 8.8-17.5]), and ten completed the longitudinal intervention protocol. The protocol comprised two medical-food interventions separated by washout periods: MF1 contained alpha-lactalbumin, inulin, and fructo-oligosaccharides, whereas MF2 contained the MF1 formulation supplemented with sodium butyrate. Clinical assessments, gut microbiota profiling, and fecal and systemic fatty acid measurements were performed at predefined study time points.
RESULTS: Seizure response varied substantially between participants. Two subjects showed a 52% and 57% reduction in monthly seizure frequency during MF1, whereas two different participants experienced reductions greater than 90% during MF2 (94% and 100%, respectively). At the cohort level, the lowest median seizure frequency was observed at the final study time point. A progressive decrease in CDD severity scale scores was also observed over the course of the study. Intervention phases coincided with transient enrichment of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing genera, including Faecalibacterium, Blautia, and Dorea. Microbiota composition differed between responders and non-responders: higher seizure burden was linked to increased Veillonella, whereas lower seizure frequency corresponded to enrichment of Dialister and Gemmiger. Fecal and systemic SCFA concentrations generally decreased during intervention phases, regardless of clinical response.
SIGNIFICANCE: Overall, these findings support a possible interaction between nutritional supplementation, microbial dynamics, and clinical manifestations in CDD. Larger studies will be necessary to clarify the therapeutic relevance of personalized microbiota-targeted approaches in CDD-related epilepsy.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) is a rare condition that causes severe developmental difficulties and seizures that are difficult to control. We studied whether two medical food interventions targeting the gut microbiota, one of which also contained sodium butyrate, could influence seizures, disease severity, gut microbiota composition, and metabolite production in people with CDD. Some participants experienced substantial reductions in seizure frequency alongside changes in gut bacteria, although responses varied considerably between individuals. These preliminary findings suggest that microbiota-targeted, non-pharmacological approaches may have potential as supportive strategies in CDD, but larger studies are needed to confirm these observations.

INTRODUCTION: Neuromodulation technologies have emerged as promising tools to enhance motor recovery following ischemic stroke. Acute reperfusion therapy remains highly time-dependent, underscoring the need for interventions that augment post-stroke neuroplasticity. Brain stimulation techniques aim to modulate cortical excitability and promote adaptive reorganization of motor networks during the critical recovery period after stroke.
AREAS COVERED: The authors review recent advances in neuromodulation strategies for post-stroke motor recovery, as well as the key principles underlying neuromodulation. Major noninvasive modalities, including transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and low-intensity focused ultrasound stimulation (LIFUS), are reviewed alongside emerging applications of invasive techniques such as deep brain stimulation (DBS) and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS). Recent randomized clinical trials and translational studies are also highlighted. This article is based on literature obtained through PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov searches for content published between 1 January 2020 and 30 March 202630 March 2026 and was supplemented by earlier landmark studies relevant to stroke recovery and neuromodulation.
EXPERT OPINION: Although neuromodulation technologies demonstrate encouraging safety profiles, clinical trial results feature notable neutral results. Future studies bear the burden of refining stimulation paradigms, patient selection, and rehabilitation dosing, possibly leveraging personalized, biomarker-driven patient selection.

papers.title: Recent Advances in Wearable Ultrasound Patches for Healthcare Applications.
papers.abstract: Wearable ultrasound patches, as a transformative innovation redefining the boundaries of traditional ultrasound medicine, signify a shift from hospital-centered, episodic diagnosis and therapy toward portable, personalized, and continuous healthcare solutions. As an emerging and rapidly evolving research direction, fully integrated wearable ultrasound platforms-synergistically combining real-time imaging, closed-loop sensing, and on-demand therapeutic intervention within a single conformal patch and system-have been progressively utilized for chronic disease management and closed-loop neuromodulation. This review summarizes and discusses the advanced wearable ultrasound technologies to provide insight into the underlying strategies that enable the convergence of diagnosis and therapy in diverse disease scenarios. This review primarily focuses on wearable ultrasound patches and systems for cardiovascular monitoring, musculoskeletal assessment, neurological treatment, sonodynamic therapy, drug delivery, and integrated theranostics. In addition, the challenges and development prospects of wearable ultrasound patches are analyzed to promote further clinical translation, with emphasis on the synergistic optimization of imaging and therapy, long-term integration reliability, and fully integrated portable designs. It is earnestly expected that this kind of flexible-electronics-enabled wearable ultrasound technology will stimulate comprehensive investigation and promote the clinical development of next-generation multifunctional theranostic platforms.

papers.title: Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation in pediatric epileptic syndromes: mechanisms, limitations, and future research horizons.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Drug-resistant epilepsy affects approximately 20 to 30% of children with epilepsy, with particularly devastating outcomes in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs). Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation (c-tDCS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation approach warranting systematic evaluation.
STATE OF THE ART: Recent meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials demonstrate significant reductions in seizure frequency following c-tDCS compared with sham stimulation, corresponding to roughly 3 to 4 fewer seizures per month or a proportional reduction of about 45% at 4 weeks. Evidence supports efficacy in focal epilepsies and selected syndromes, including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and early-onset epileptic encephalopathies. Standard protocols employ 1 to 2 mA cathodal stimulation for 20 minutes over 5 to 10 consecutive sessions. High-definition tDCS configurations allow more focal current delivery. However, significant inter-individual variability exists, and the relationship between interictal epileptiform discharge suppression and clinical seizure outcomes remains inconsistent. Computational modeling demonstrates substantially higher cortical electric field strengths in children than in adults at equivalent current intensities, raising important dosing considerations. Safety data from over 600 pediatric sessions indicate favorable tolerability with no serious adverse events, although seizure exacerbation has been reported in a minority of participants in open-label studies.
CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: Cathodal tDCS represents a safe, tolerable, and potentially effective adjunct to unchanged antiseizure medication regimens in children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and should presently be regarded as investigational. Selection criteria, optimal stimulation parameters, and syndrome-specific protocols require further refinement. Particular caution is warranted with transcranial alternating current stimulation in generalized epilepsies.
FUTURE DIRECTIONS: Research priorities include closed-loop electroencephalography (EEG)-triggered stimulation systems, biomarker- driven patient selection, age-appropriate dosimetry informed by computational modeling, and adequately powered trials in specific DEE populations including West syndrome, Dravet syndrome, and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation during sleep.

papers.title: An amygdala-mediated simulation-to-decision cascade aligns interbrain dynamics to solve social dilemmas.
papers.title_zh: 杏仁核介导的模拟决策级联使大脑间动力学保持一致，以解决社会困境。
papers.abstract: Mutual cooperation (MC) requires independent decision-makers to coordinate under uncertainty about each other's intentions. Using simultaneous intracranial electroencephalography from epilepsy-patient dyads playing a real-time iterated prisoner's dilemma, we identified neurocognitive mechanisms that enable interacting brains to align during mutual cooperation. Amygdala interbrain representational alignment (IBRA), similarity in fine-grained neural spectral patterns across partners, emerged selectively during MC and predicted trial-by-trial outcomes. Early θ-suppression-characterized IBRA reflected rapid, history-sensitive alignment, whereas later IBRA, characterized by low-frequency suppression and γ increases, supported coordinated commitment and action. Furthermore, mutual cooperation relied on an amygdala-mediated, simulation-to-decision cascade, operationalized here as a model-based prospective estimate of partner cooperation that guided self-choice. Amygdala low-frequency suppression tracked this prospective estimate of partner cooperation and θ-γ coupling linked this partner estimate to self-decision processes. Conditional cooperators strategically relied on partner tracking, whereas unconditional cooperators leveraged dispositional tolerance of uncertainty to transition into anticipatory neural alignment. These findings reveal the neural interdependency underpinning MC, redefining cooperation not as isolated decision-making but as a dynamic, interbrain, cognitive alignment.

papers.title: Vascular Risk Factors and Late-Onset Epilepsy.
papers.title_zh: 血管危险因素和晚发性癫痫。
papers.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Late-onset epilepsy (LOE; onset at age ≥65 years) is increasingly recognized in older adults and may be associated with vascular risk.
OBJECTIVE: To identify vascular risk factors (VRFs) associated with incident LOE in older adults.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This study is an individual participant data meta-analysis of 6 US population-based prospective cohort studies (the Epilepsy-Cog Study). In 5 cohorts linked to Medicare for epilepsy case ascertainment, follow-up for LOE began when a participant had accrued 2 years of continuous fee-for-service enrollment and was 65 years of age or older and extended to the end of continuous enrollment. Claims linkage covered 1991-2018 in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study (ARIC), 1992-2019 in the Cardiovascular Health Study (CHS), 2000-2019 in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), 2000-2020 in the Reasons for Geographic and Racial Differences in Stroke Study (REGARDS), and 1999-2019 in the Washington Heights/Inwood Columbia Aging Project (WHICAP). In the Northern Manhattan Study (NOMAS), which was not Medicare linked and used cohort-based epilepsy case ascertainment, follow-up for LOE began at cohort entry in 1993-2008 and extended to 2024. Data analysis was completed in January 2026.
EXPOSURES: Sociodemographic characteristics and VRFs assessed by self-report, examinations, laboratory measures, and medication use.
MAIN OUTCOME AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was incident LOE. Associations between risk factors and incident LOE were evaluated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models to estimate hazard ratios.
RESULTS: From 43 753 participants in Epilepsy-Cog, 551 participants with prevalent epilepsy and 945 with no follow-up after Epilepsy-Cog baseline were excluded. Among 42 257 participants (mean [SD] age, 71.4 [6.9] years; 23 383 [56.0%] female) followed up for a mean (SD) of 9.3 (6.2) years, 1500 participants (3.5%) developed LOE (3.8 per 1000 person-years). In fully adjusted models, LOE risk was higher with current smoking (HR = 1.39; 95% CI, 1.18-1.64), hypertension (HR = 1.17; 95% CI, 1.04-1.31), diabetes (HR = 1.42; 95% CI, 1.25-1.62), chronic kidney disease (HR = 1.29; 95% CI, 1.13-1.48), history of stroke (HR = 1.99; 95% CI, 1.63-2.43), and apolipoprotein E ε4 allele (1 ε4 allele: HR = 1.22; 95% CI, 1.07-1.39; 2 ε4 alleles: HR = 1.84; 95% CI, 1.36-2.50). Associations of VRFs with LOE were similar across age, sex, and race and ethnicity subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this pooled analysis of 6 US cohorts, multiple VRFs and a history of stroke were associated with incident LOE. These findings suggest that LOE may reflect the underlying burden of brain vascular disease.

papers.title: Progressive Hippocampal Volume Reduction Beyond Normal Aging in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: A Longitudinal MRI Study.

papers.abstract: Recent neuroimaging studies have suggested that epilepsy may show progressive brain structural changes over time. However, longitudinal hippocampal volume changes in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) have not been adequately compared with those observed in normal aging. In this study, we enrolled 46 patients with unilateral TLE and 25 healthy controls with longitudinal structural MRI scans using the same scanner. Hippocampal volumes were quantified using the Hipposeg software, and the annual percentage volume reduction relative to baseline (%Reduction/year) was calculated for each hippocampus. Compared to healthy hippocampi (median -0.37% per year, IQR = 3.97), both ipsilateral (median -1.04% per year, IQR = 3.65) and contralateral (median -1.08% per year, IQR = 3.17) hippocampi in TLE showed significantly greater volume reduction over time (both p < 0.05). Furthermore, annual ipsilateral hippocampal volume reduction was significantly correlated with disease duration (Spearman's rs = 0.366, FDR-corrected p = 0.036), suggesting that hippocampal atrophy progresses more rapidly during the early stage after epilepsy onset. These findings indicate that hippocampal volume loss in TLE exceeds that expected from normal aging and provide further evidence supporting progressive structural alterations during the course of the disease. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Temporal lobe epilepsy may cause progressive changes in the brain beyond those expected from normal aging. Using repeated MRI scans, we found that the hippocampus showed greater volume loss over time in people with temporal lobe epilepsy than in healthy individuals. This volume loss occurred bilaterally and appeared to be greater during the earlier stages of the disease. These results provide further evidence supporting progressive structural brain changes in TLE and contribute to a better understanding of disease progression and abnormal brain aging in epilepsy.

papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Characterization of early neuropsychological outcomes following SEEG with radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RFTHC) is essential to guide patient expectations around return to work, study, and caregiving. The current study aimed to describe the early neurocognitive sequelae of SEEG.
METHODS: Consecutive patients undergoing SEEG were prospectively recruited from two tertiary epilepsy centers in Melbourne, Australia. Patients were administered the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS) via telehealth before and 3 weeks after SEEG (M = 19.69 days, SD = 4.41). Given the telehealth platform, the coding subtest was substituted for the Symbol Digit Modalities Test, and a modified score of global cognitive function was calculated. To evaluate group changes, paired sample t-tests were performed. Reliable change indices were computed to explore individual-level changes. Pearson's correlation coefficients evaluated relationships between change in global cognitive function and SEEG admission variables. SEEG patients were invited to complete a semi-structured interview canvassing the recovery following SEEG.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight patients completed the neuropsychological examination (M = 37.89 years, SD = 9.72, range = 17-56 years, 54% female). All patients underwent RFTHC with a mean of 11.43 (SD = 6.87, range = 2-28) coagulation sites. At a whole group level, 3-weeks post SEEG there was no evidence for global nor domain-specific cognitive change. Reliable change indices with 90% confidence revealed only 4% (1/28) declined on at least two measures and 10% (3/28) showed psychometric improvement. Pearson's correlational coefficients showed no evidence for association between change in global cognitive function with SEEG factors including admission length, number of spontaneous or stimulated seizures, number of electrodes, or number of RFTHC sites. Subjective reports of language change tended to be accompanied by a decline on the RBANS language index that did not meet reliable change criteria. Most patients reported returning to work around 4 weeks post SEEG.
SIGNIFICANCE: By 3 weeks, gross cognitive functioning tends to be in keeping with pre-SEEG performances for most patients. These findings have direct clinical implications for SEEG neuropsychological counseling.
PLAIN LANGUAGE STATEMENT: SEEG is increasingly used to guide epilepsy surgery. Despite this, little is known about the cognitive recovery in the weeks following the procedure. We found that for most patients, broad cognitive functioning 3 weeks after SEEG with coagulation was consistent with function before SEEG, with only a small minority showing significant changes. Some people who reported language difficulties also showed a decline on language testing, although this was often small. Of those patients working before SEEG, most returned to work by 4 weeks. These results provide important evidence to guide patient counseling, recovery planning, and management after SEEG.

papers.title: Validation of the diagnosis of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: Challenges and lessons learned.
papers.title_zh: Lennox-Gastaut综合征诊断的验证：挑战和经验教训。
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome (LGS) is a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by multiple seizure types, cognitive impairment, and distinct electroencephalographic (EEG) findings. However, evolving diagnostic criteria, heterogeneous clinical features, and inconsistent electronic health record (EHR) documentation complicate accurate diagnosis and cohort identification. As part of a Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute-sponsored study developing EHR-based computable phenotypes for LGS, we established a reference standard through retrospective chart review and epileptologist classification.
METHODS: A multicenter retrospective chart review was conducted across seven pediatric epilepsy centers. Stratified sampling using PCORnet data selected patients based on the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision diagnosis code for LGS or other intractable epilepsy diagnoses between 2016 and 2022. Clinical teams abstracted seizure history, EEG findings, developmental status, and treatment history. Two epileptologists independently reviewed each case as classic LGS, pragmatic LGS, or not LGS. Discordant cases underwent adjudication by a senior epileptologist. Cases with incomplete or unclear data underwent repeat abstraction and review.
RESULTS: Of 997 identified patients, 935 underwent classification after exclusions. Initial epileptologist disagreement occurred in 105 cases (11%, unweighted Cohen kappa = 82%). Following adjudication, 130 cases underwent reabstraction to retrieve additional EEG reports and clinical details. Rereview reclassified 67 cases initially considered "not LGS": 33 classic LGS, 12 pragmatic LGS, and 22 excluded for insufficient data. Key EHR challenges included inconsistent EEG reporting, incomplete seizure type characterization, fragmented documentation of cognitive impairment, unclear age at onset, and variable terminology across institutions and providers. Slow spike-and-wave EEG findings were the most frequently missing diagnostic element.
SIGNIFICANCE: Validating LGS diagnoses using EHR data is complex and resource intensive. Standardized terminology, structured documentation, and rigorous multicenter validation may improve diagnostic accuracy, research cohort identification, computable phenotype development, and longitudinal care for individuals with LGS. Our results highlight important operational lessons for multicenter rare epilepsy studies and underscore the need for improved diagnosis pathways and longitudinal care systems for those with LGS and their families.

papers.title: Beyond neuroprotection: Context-dependent effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists on seizure susceptibility.
papers.title_zh: 超越神经保护： GLP-1受体激动剂对癫痫易感性的上下文依赖性影响。
papers.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used in type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity and are increasingly considered to exert neuroprotective effects. Recent large-scale clinical and real-world studies report a predominantly neutral to protective association between GLP-1 RA use and seizure- or epilepsy-related diagnoses. However, how these agents affect neuronal excitability in patients with established epileptogenic networks remains insufficiently understood. This narrative review critically examines the experimental and clinical evidence from GLP-1 RA effects on neuronal excitability and seizure susceptibility, with a focus on possible discrepancies between population-level outcomes and individual network-level vulnerability. Preclinical studies demonstrate heterogeneous, network-dependent effects of GLP-1 RAs. Although anticonvulsant and neuroprotective properties are observed in chemically induced seizure models, paradoxical pro-seizure effects occur in genetic absence epilepsy models. In contrast, population-level analyses report neutral to reduced rates of incident epilepsy or seizure-related outcomes under GLP-1 RA therapy. However, these findings are based largely on administrative diagnostic codes, lack epileptological phenotyping, and are not designed to capture transient, exposure-dependent alterations in neuronal excitability or short-term seizure dynamics. Additional factors, including delayed gastric emptying affecting anti-seizure medication absorption, rapid metabolic shifts during titration, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and agent-specific pharmacokinetics, may further modulate individual susceptibility. We propose that GLP-1 RA effects on neuronal excitability are context dependent, shaped by epilepsy subtype, network vulnerability, exposure dynamics, and treatment phase. Targeted prospective studies incorporating clinical phenotyping, therapeutic drug monitoring, and temporal seizure assessment are required to ensure neurological safety in patients with epilepsy.

papers.title: The translational asymmetry of corpus callosotomy: Two literatures that answered different questions.
papers.title_zh: 痂体切开术的翻译不对称性：两篇回答不同问题的文献。
papers.abstract: Corpus callosotomy is an established palliative operation for drug-resistant epilepsy dominated by drop attacks, and it is performed in three extents: anterior, usually of the anterior two-thirds; total, in one or two stages; and selective posterior, which preserves the genu and rostral body. Meta-analysis finds no difference between them in overall seizure reduction, a difference in drop attack control favoring the posterior approach, and a graded difference in disconnection syndrome, but there has never been a prospective head-to-head comparison, and the optimal extent of section remains undefined. A search of PubMed, Embase, and the Web of Science Core Collection identified 62 experimental studies in which the corpus callosum or another forebrain commissure was sectioned with an epilepsy-related outcome, spanning 1948-2026 across six species and every major seizure model. This literature is neither absent nor recent. What it has almost never done is vary the extent of section: the few studies that varied it took the laterality of kindling transfer or of interictal synchrony as the endpoint, never seizure control and never cognitive cost. No study compares the three extents against a common outcome; none models the selective posterior operation as it is defined clinically; none randomizes between extents; and none combines graded disconnection with time-locked bilateral electrophysiology, diffusion-based verification of the fibers divided, and a behavioral read-out in the same animals. The effect of section is also bidirectional: focal seizures may intensify through loss of transcallosal inhibition, and in the pentylenetetrazol model callosal section paradoxically facilitates convulsions, which limits chemoconvulsant preparations. The asymmetry between the clinical and experimental literatures is therefore one of method rather than of volume or attention: the two answered different questions, and the question the clinical field now asks requires a manipulation the experimental literature has never performed. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Surgeons can treat severe epilepsies by cutting the bundle of fibers that joins the two halves of the brain, but they do not agree on how much of it to cut. We searched three databases and found 62 animal studies of this operation going back to 1948. Almost none of them compared different amounts of cutting, and none looked at the newest version of the operation. Answering the surgeons' question will require a new kind of animal experiment rather than more reading of the old ones.

papers.title: Symptom-related damage patterns in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study was undertaken to elucidate the neuroanatomical and network substrates underlying diverse seizure symptoms in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis (mTLE-HS) by applying multivariate support vector regression (SVR) to individualized structural symptom mapping and atrophy network mapping (ANM).
METHODS: We retrospectively enrolled 216 patients with mTLE-HS and 460 healthy controls. Six non-mutually exclusive seizure symptoms were assessed. We performed left-right flipping of all images of right-sided mTLE-HS patients along the midline before processing the data. Individual atrophy gray matter maps were derived using normative modeling. Structural symptom mapping was performed using multivariate SVR lesion-symptom mapping. For each patient, indirect ANM maps were generated using a normative functional connectome and direct ANM maps using the patient's own resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Correspondence between the two ANM approaches was assessed using individual-level whole-brain spatial correlations of unthresholded maps and group-level Dice coefficients of thresholded maps.
RESULTS: Individual structural atrophy patterns were spatially heterogeneous, whereas different seizure manifestations were associated with partially distinct structural patterns and more spatially convergent network-level associations. Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures were associated with thalamic network involvement, gestural/limb automatisms with anterior cingulate-related networks, ictal vocalization symptoms with perisylvian language networks, dysmnesia with hippocampal-posteromedial networks, emotional phenomena with prefrontal-temporal networks, and autonomic phenomena with medial prefrontal and limbic networks. Furthermore, limited spatial correspondence was observed between the results of the direct and indirect atrophy network analyses, suggesting the indirect and direct ANM can be regarded as nonequivalent but potentially complementary approaches.
SIGNIFICANCE: In mTLE-HS, heterogeneous seizure manifestations are associated with distinct patterns of atrophy and distributed functional network involvement. ANM provides a complementary framework for characterizing symptom-related network patterns, and differences between indirect/normative and direct/patient-specific connectome analyses may provide complementary information.

papers.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding.
papers.abstract: Objective . Speech Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach . Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results . We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. In contrast, there are significant overlaps in signal timings contributing to EEG-based decoding, regardless of vocal conditions such as overt or covert speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance . Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.&#xD.

papers.title: Sleep Spindles and Slow Oscillations as Potential Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets in Mild-to-Moderate Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review critically evaluates evidence on sleep spindles (SP), slow oscillations (SOs), and their coordination in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD), focusing on their relationships with cognition, AD biomarkers, and their therapeutic potential.
RECENT FINDINGS: Longitudinal studies associate greater SP and/or SO activity with better cognition and favourable amyloid and tau profiles after clinical onset. Spindle and SO coupling may index network integrity. Preserved NREM sleep oscillations are associated with lower orexin concentrations and weaker adverse relationships between orexin and cognitive and neuropsychiatric outcomes. Closed-loop acoustic stimulation and slow-oscillatory transcranial direct-current stimulation can modify SO activity, spindle activity, and coupling, although cognitive and biomarker benefits remain uncertain. Spindle-SO activity, including their temporal coupling, are associated with cognition and AD biomarkers across the disease continuum. Closed-loop acoustic and electrical stimulation can modify these oscillations, but biomarker-characterized trials in MCI and AD are needed to determine whether treatment produces durable cognitive and biomarker benefits.

papers.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy for depression: state-dependent mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational challenges.
papers.abstract: Depression is a highly prevalent and debilitating mental disorder. Pharmacotherapy remains the primary treatment modality; however, its efficacy is often limited by a delayed onset of action, suboptimal response in some patients, and a high risk of recurrence. Treatment-resistant depression, characterized by poor response to conventional therapies, poses a major clinical challenge and highlights the need for improved treatment strategies. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for depression, particularly when combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy. Advances in neuroimaging, neurochemistry, and network neuroscience have clarified how high-frequency rTMS may modulate cortical excitability, monoaminergic transmission, synaptic plasticity, and distributed brain networks. Clinical evidence suggests that combined treatment may accelerate early improvement, increase response and remission, and reduce relapse risk; however, these benefits are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains and should be interpreted in light of expectancy effects and limitations of sham blinding. Neuroimaging studies have identified treatment-associated functional and structural changes, including hippocampal volume changes, but the causal links among molecular signaling, circuit reorganization, structural findings, and symptom improvement remain unresolved. The interaction between rTMS and antidepressants should therefore not be viewed as uniformly additive or synergistic, but as a state-dependent process shaped by medication class, stimulation protocol and timing, cortical excitability, metaplasticity, and individual neurobiological context. This review integrates mechanistic, neuroimaging, and clinical evidence and discusses how biomarker-, state-, and symptom-informed targeting, optimized treatment sequencing, and pragmatic implementation strategies could improve the precision and accessibility of combined treatment for depression.
